questions.question: At 1.5 million operations per second, 80% reads, and a 90% read hit rate, how many reads per second reach the backing store?
options: 15,000 reads per second
120,000 reads per second
150,000 reads per second
300,000 reads per second
questions.explanation: Read traffic is 1.5M x 0.8 = 1.2M reads/s. A 10% miss rate sends 120K reads/s to the backing store.

questions.question: A 2 TB logical working set uses replication factor 2. What is its cache memory footprint before headroom and allocator overhead?
options: 1 TB
2 TB
4 TB
6 TB
questions.explanation: Replication factor 2 stores two copies of each cached value, so 2 TB of logical data consumes 4 TB before operational headroom.

questions.question: Why use consistent hashing with virtual nodes when adding cache capacity?
options: It guarantees every physical node receives exactly the same number of requests.
It allows the client to skip all cluster membership metadata.
It moves only the ranges claimed by the new node and smooths ownership across physical nodes.
It makes replication and failover unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing limits remapping during membership changes, while virtual nodes reduce skew by giving each physical node many small ranges.

questions.question: A primary acknowledges a write before its asynchronous replica applies it, then the primary fails. What can a replica read observe?
options: It is guaranteed to see the acknowledged value immediately.
It may return an older value until replication catches up, or lose the unreplicated cache update.
It must query every cache node before responding.
It permanently corrupts the backing database.
questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication improves latency but permits a lag window. The cache contract must tolerate staleness or use a stronger mode for selected namespaces.

questions.question: Which eviction policy is usually the better starting point when a small stable hot set is mixed with large one-time scans?
options: FIFO, because insertion order captures popularity
Random eviction, because all values have equal reuse probability
LRU without admission control, because scans should replace the entire cache
LFU with aging or an admission policy, because repeated frequency should survive scan pollution
questions.explanation: A scan can make one-time values look recent and evict useful entries under plain LRU. Frequency with aging or explicit admission better protects a stable hot set.

questions.question: One popular key expires while 100 requests arrive together. What most directly prevents 100 backing store reads?
options: Increase the key length
Coalesce concurrent fills for that key and apply a bounded origin fallback budget
Rehash the entire cluster immediately
Retry every miss from every client without a deadline
questions.explanation: Single-flight request coalescing lets one request load the value while the other requests await that result. Admission limits keep the miss path bounded.

questions.question: During a network partition, what prevents the isolated old owner and a promoted replica from both accepting writes for the same key range?
options: A higher ring epoch or fencing token enforced by storage and clients
A longer cache TTL
More virtual nodes without versioning
Average CPU utilization below 50%
questions.explanation: Health checks detect reachability, not authority. Enforcing a newer epoch or fencing token makes stale owners unable to commit writes.

questions.question: P99 latency rises while hit rate falls, evictions increase, and backing store QPS climbs. What should the on-call engineer investigate first?
options: Whether cache memory pressure, expiration waves, or rebalancing is creating a miss storm
Whether average response size changed by one byte
Whether the quiz service is unavailable
Whether to disable all cache metrics
questions.explanation: Those signals form a causal chain from cache churn to misses, origin load, and tail latency. Check memory, TTL behavior, hot keys, and recent topology movement together.
